content_voiceover: This is the practical surgical management table for VWD, worth memorizing the logic rather than every number. For type 1, desmopressin is first line, given IV or subcutaneously at 0.3 micrograms per kilogram, or intranasally at 300 micrograms, that's 150 micrograms per nostril, plus tranexamic acid as an adjunct. For type 2, you can still try desmopressin or go straight to VWF concentrate, but remember the critical exception, DDAVP is contraindicated in type 2B, because it can worsen thrombocytopenia by releasing more of the abnormal high-affinity VWF that binds platelets. Type 3 has no endogenous VWF to release, so it always requires VWF or factor VIII concentrate, never DDAVP. For concentrate dosing, the bigger the procedure, the higher the target and the longer the duration, dental extraction needs 25 IU per kilogram with a peak above 50 for just one day, minor surgery needs a peak above 80 with trough above 50 for 3 to 5 days, and major surgery needs a peak above 100 on day one, tapering troughs down to 30 by days 7 through 10, since duration lasts a full week to ten days.
keypoints: Type 1: DDAVP (IV/SC 0.3 mcg/kg or intranasal 150 mcg/nostril) + TXA
Type 2: DDAVP or VWF concentrate + TXA - DDAVP CONTRAINDICATED in 2B
Type 3: VWF/FVIII concentrate only (no endogenous VWF to release)
Major surgery: peak VWF:Act >=100 IU/dL, taper trough to >=30 by day 7-10
keypoint_voiceover: For surgical VWD management, type 1 gets desmopressin plus tranexamic acid. Type 2 can use desmopressin or VWF concentrate, but never DDAVP in type 2B, since it can worsen thrombocytopenia. Type 3 always needs VWF or factor VIII concentrate since there's no endogenous VWF to mobilize. Dosing and duration scale with procedure size, from a single day for dental extraction up to seven to ten days for major surgery.
